primary_cause: Post-earnings fade from Micron March 25 report with investors looking past the beat and focusing on uncertain memory demand into lockdown. Revenue $4.80B and non-GAAP EPS $0.45 with Q3 guided to $5.2B but collapsing end-demand visibility
secondary_factors: Semiconductor beta and market renewed skepticism after three-day stimulus rally ended
store_description: Micron had posted $4.80B of Q2 revenue and $0.45 of adjusted EPS on March 25 with Q3 revenue guided to about $5.2B but that did not fully offset investor concern that COVID-19 would damage near-term demand in consumer and industrial end markets. By March 31 MU was still trading more like a cyclical memory name than a defensive stay-at-home tech winner.

primary_cause: Bank-sector recession risk not a Goldman-specific event. End of relief rally on March 27 and growing recession fears heading into quarter-end
secondary_factors: Expectations for weaker dealmaking more loan-loss provisioning across the system and quarter-end de-risking
store_description: GS traded like a macro bank broker on March 31. As investors reassessed the economic damage from COVID-19 and then saw initial jobless claims explode to 6.648M sentiment turned against economically sensitive financials even without a fresh Goldman-specific bombshell.

primary_cause: Recession and brick-and-mortar exposure fears. No strong Home Depot-specific negative Reuters item in prior 3 days. Mounting concern around real economy consumer spending and store-traffic disruption
secondary_factors: Investors rotating away from cyclical retail after March rebound
store_description: Home Depot sold off as investors priced in the possibility that lockdowns would choke discretionary home-improvement demand and complicate store operations even though the business would later prove more resilient than feared. The key swing factor was worsening U.S. labor-market damage.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Accenture reported March 19 and cut full-year local-currency revenue growth guidance to 3%-6% from 6%-8% and lowered EPS guidance to $7.48-$7.70 from $7.66-$7.84 because of coronavirus uncertainty
secondary_factors: Broader fear that enterprise IT and consulting budgets would be delayed or canceled
store_description: ACN March 31 decline looks most tied to the market continuing to digest its March 19 outlook reset where management explicitly baked in COVID disruption and trimmed expected 2020 revenue growth to 3%-6%. Investors were increasingly assuming consulting transformation work and discretionary enterprise projects would be pushed out.

primary_cause: Semiconductor cycle and recession fear not a distinct company event. No clean Applied Materials-specific negative headline in prior 3 days. Equipment names being repriced for global capex slowdown
secondary_factors: China supply-chain uncertainty and concern that memory and foundry customers would slow spending
store_description: AMAT drop looks more like group weakness than company-specific damage. As the March rebound stalled investors again focused on whether chipmakers and foundries would cut capital spending into a sudden global recession a direct risk to wafer-fab equipment suppliers.

primary_cause: High-beta semiconductor selloff as investors re-priced global demand risk. No strong AMD-only negative item in prior 3 days. Pressure mostly reversal in risk appetite across high-beta semis after March 24-26 rebound
secondary_factors: Fear of weaker PC gaming and enterprise hardware demand if lockdowns deepened
store_description: AMD fell harder than the index because it was a higher-beta semiconductor name that had bounced sharply and was vulnerable to renewed demand fears. With investors reassessing how long the shutdown would last cyclical growth semis were sold even without fresh company-specific news.

primary_cause: Consumer-credit and travel-spending risk overwhelming a neutral-to-slightly positive company update. On March 30 Reuters reported American Express said it would avoid job cuts in 2020 but that was not enough to offset growing fear around T&E spending and card delinquencies
secondary_factors: Coming wave of unemployment and concern over charge-offs and reserve builds
store_description: Even though AmEx told employees on March 30 it would avoid layoffs in 2020 investors were focused on the much bigger issue: a near-freeze in travel and entertainment spend plus rising credit losses. As the labor market deteriorated toward 6.648M weekly jobless claims AXP was treated as one of the most exposed consumer-finance names.

primary_cause: Sector-wide bank credit-loss fears. No clear BAC-specific negative headline in prior 3 days. Dominant news was worsening recession risk and mounting expectation of large credit provisions
secondary_factors: Near-zero rates compressed NIM and quarter-end positioning
store_description: BAC traded as a classic credit-cycle bank into quarter-end. The combination of collapsing rates recession expectations and the following week 6.648M jobless-claims figure made investors anticipate sharply higher reserve builds and lower profitability.

primary_cause: Rotation out of rate-sensitive REITs and defensive yield plays as sharp late-March rally stalled. No distinct American Tower headline in prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Broad deleveraging and concern that tenants globally could face stress even in relatively resilient infrastructure categories
store_description: AMT move looks disproportionately large relative to the index but could not be pinned to a clean stock-specific news event. The most plausible explanation is a sharp rotation out of REITs and rate-sensitive defensives into quarter-end layered on top of generalized balance-sheet stress.

primary_cause: Bank-sector credit and recession fears. No obvious Citi-only negative headline in prior 3 days. Worsening macro damage and fear of elevated provisioning across money-center banks
secondary_factors: Global consumer and corporate exposure and quarter-end de-risking
store_description: Citi international and card exposure made it especially sensitive to a synchronized global shutdown. Into March 31 investors were increasingly pricing in severe reserve builds and weaker capital-markets activity despite policy support.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. NBCUniversal had previously sold record $1.25B in Tokyo Olympics advertising and Olympics were postponed on March 24 throwing ad inventory and pricing into limbo. Also faced theme-park and advertising weakness
secondary_factors: Theme-park shutdowns and broader ad-spending cuts
store_description: CMCSA decline is best explained by worsening visibility at NBCUniversal: the Olympics postponement disrupted a record $1.25B ad-sales haul while the broader advertising market was weakening fast as marketers cut budgets. The stock was also absorbing the revenue hit from theme-park closures.

primary_cause: Consumer-credit deterioration fears. No Capital One-specific Reuters headline in prior 3 days but macro news especially bad for card lenders because unemployment was exploding
secondary_factors: Exposure to lower-FICO borrowers higher expected charge-offs and reserve builds
store_description: COF fell more than the big money-center banks because investors viewed card-heavy lenders as direct casualties of lockdown-driven job losses. The following report of 6.648M weekly jobless claims validated the concern that delinquencies and charge-offs would spike.

primary_cause: Multiple compression and software de-risking after late-March rally. No strong Salesforce-specific negative item in prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Concern that enterprise customers would slow new software spending even if mission-critical subscriptions held up
store_description: CRM decline looks more like a valuation and risk-off move than a company-specific shock. Investors were trying to distinguish between resilient recurring-software revenue and weaker new-seat services and upsell demand as businesses scrambled to cut discretionary spending.

primary_cause: Ongoing theme-park and entertainment shutdown damage. Reuters reported shortly after on April 2 that Disney would furlough some U.S. employees confirming severity of shutdown impact. Market already knew parks and cruises effectively shut
secondary_factors: ESPN and sports disruption and advertising weakness
store_description: DIS was still being repriced for a near-total halt in several of its highest-operating-leverage businesses. The April 2 furlough announcement did not create the problem so much as confirm what investors were already assuming on March 31: a prolonged earnings collapse across parks cruises theatrical releases and sports media.

primary_cause: Rotation out of defensive utilities as market rebound faltered and investors rebalanced quarter-end positions. No clear Duke-specific negative headline in prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Concern about commercial and industrial power demand weakness in lockdown economy
store_description: DUK move appears mostly macro and positioning-driven rather than headline-driven. Utilities were not at the epicenter of the COVID shock but investors still had reason to worry about weaker electricity demand from businesses and about indiscriminate selling into quarter-end.

primary_cause: Asset-manager sensitivity to falling markets and credit stress. No BlackRock-specific negative Reuters article in prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Pressure on AUM ETF volatility and generalized financial-sector selling
store_description: BLK traded down with financials as investors focused on what a violent Q1 and stressed credit markets would mean for fee-bearing assets and risk sentiment. No discrete company event in the March 28-31 window strong enough to beat the simpler explanation of falling markets and quarter-end financial-sector selling.

primary_cause: Digital-ad demand fears plus April 1 macro shock. Reuters later reported coronavirus led to sudden ad-budget cuts across travel retail and entertainment advertisers. Trump warned of painful two weeks ahead
secondary_factors: Broad tech selloff and uncertainty around SMB advertiser health
store_description: Facebook dropped as investors realized that even dominant digital ad platforms were not insulated from the abrupt stop in travel local and retail marketing spend. The stock-specific ad-risk narrative met a brutal macro tape on April 1 when Trump warned of a painful stretch ahead.

primary_cause: Post-earnings demand skepticism amplified by April 1 market washout. Investors still digesting Micron March 25 earnings and guidance but April 1 added much worse macro tape
secondary_factors: Semiconductor cyclicality and worsening economic data fears
store_description: Micron had reported $4.80B in Q2 revenue and guided Q3 to about $5.2B but the stock still traded as a cyclical memory supplier into an intensifying shutdown. On April 1 that company-specific skepticism was compounded by a broad market plunge after the White House warned of a grim virus trajectory.

primary_cause: Macro-led tech selloff not a Microsoft-specific deterioration. On March 31 Reuters reported Microsoft had seen 775% jump in Teams calling and meetings in Italy underscoring strong remote-work demand but overshadowed by broader market shock
secondary_factors: Concern that cloud capacity strain and enterprise spending caution could limit near-term upside despite strong usage growth
store_description: Microsoft actually had supportive product-usage news going into the drop with Teams activity in Italy up 775% over a month. The stock still fell because April 1 was a market-wide derisking day driven by grim COVID projections and even relatively defensive mega-cap tech was sold.

primary_cause: Pure financial-sector panic over recession depth and credit losses. No Morgan Stanley-specific headline in prior 3 days explaining size of move better than macro. Critical backdrop was Trump painful warning and jobless claims explosion to 6.648M
secondary_factors: Expected hit to wealth-management flows investment banking and trading normalization after March volatility spike
store_description: Morgan Stanley 7.0% drop was larger than Goldman because it traded as a higher-beta financial heading into a very ugly April 1 tape. The market was rapidly shifting from policy rescue to how bad is the real economy and the answer was getting worse by the day as jobless claims surged to 6.648M.
